title: Trump Cancels Massive Iran Strike, Talks Resume Monday — Oil Tumbles 5%, Congress Targets Ankara Arms Sales
subhead: Trump called off what he called the largest planned US military operation since WWII after Gulf allies pushed for diplomacy, with US-Iran negotiations set to resume Monday afternoon. Oil crashed below $84 on de-escalation hopes. Meanwhile, a US Congress bill takes aim at Turkey's human rights record, and Erdogan reaffirms the Terror-Free Türkiye initiative as draft legislation heads to parliament.

sections.heading: Trump Calls Off 'Biggest Attack Since WWII,' US-Iran Talks Resume Monday
sections.body:
President Donald Trump said he canceled planned military strikes on Iran that he described as the largest since World War II, after Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the UAE, and Qatar urged him to pursue diplomacy instead. Fresh US-Iran negotiations are set to begin Monday afternoon, Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One. (Fox News, USA Today, Reuters)

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday that Oman-mediated negotiations over the Strait of Hormuz were in their final stages. Iran has continued to insist on controlling at least part of both shipping lanes through the strait and has sought the ability to collect fees from transiting vessels — a stance Washington strongly opposes. Iran's semi-official Mehr news agency denied that Tehran requested a pause, calling Trump's claim 'nothing but a new lie.' (News18, Arab Times, USA Today)

War Secretary Pete Hegseth said Sunday that US forces remain 'locked and loaded' and prepared to act at levels 'not seen since World War II,' underscoring that the military option has not been taken off the table. (Fox News)

For Turkiye, the stakes are direct: any breakdown in talks hits energy import costs and elevates the strategic value of the Ceyhan pipeline bypass. The last-minute de-escalation also vindicates Ankara's persistent push for diplomatic solutions — Erdogan urged both Iran and the US at the Antalya Diplomacy Forum to use the ceasefire framework to pursue lasting peace. (MSN, SANA)
sections.whyItMatters: The gap between Trump's claim of an imminent deal and Tehran's public posture is significant. If talks collapse again, the region faces a return to massive strikes and Hormuz disruption — directly threatening Turkiye's energy supply and the lira. The Ceyhan corridor gains value with every day Hormuz stays contested.

sections.heading: Oil Crashes Below $84 as De-escalation Hopes Rise, OPEC+ Adds Supply
sections.body:
Brent crude fell $4.37 (5%) to $83.56/barrel, while WTI dropped $4.63 (5.5%) to $80/barrel in early Asian trade on Monday, after Trump called off strikes and both sides signaled willingness to negotiate. The drop reverses only a fraction of July's 20%+ surge, when Hormuz disruption and Houthi attacks on Saudi oil facilities sent prices soaring. (OilPrice.com, MSN)

Adding to downward pressure, OPEC+ approved a 188,000 bpd production quota increase for September, completing the unwinding of a 1.65 million bpd voluntary cut agreed in 2023. Seven key producers — Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Kazakhstan, Algeria, and Oman — agreed to the hike. However, actual output increases may be limited by regional disruptions. (Reuters, Zee News)

Two Saudi oil tankers successfully transited the Bab el-Mandeb strait over the weekend, though the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency reported three additional tanker attacks since Saturday, keeping maritime risk elevated. (OilPrice.com, Reuters)

For Turkiye, lower oil prices provide immediate relief to the current account. The lira has lost over 18% against the dollar in the past month, partly driven by energy import costs. But the geopolitical premium remains volatile — any breakdown in Monday's talks would reverse gains quickly. (Digital Journal, Bloomberg)
sections.whyItMatters: The 5% oil price drop is a welcome reprieve for Turkiye's inflation-battered economy, but it's a snapshot of sentiment, not a structural shift. July's 20% surge is mostly intact. Turkiye's energy import bill and the lira's trajectory remain hostage to whether Monday's talks produce results.

sections.heading: US Congress Bill Targets Turkey Arms Sales Over Human Rights
sections.body:
Greek-American Congresswoman Dina Titus introduced the Turkey Human Rights Promotion Act of 2026, which would block US arms sales to Turkiye over human rights concerns. The bill joins a growing list of congressional actions placing conditions on the bilateral defense relationship. (Greek Reporter)

The legislation comes at a sensitive moment: Turkiye is simultaneously seeking to rejoin the F-35 program and deepen defense cooperation with Washington amid the Iran war, while Congress has repeatedly pushed back. The bill's specifics on which weapons systems would be affected and what human rights benchmarks Turkiye must meet remain under review. (Greek Reporter)
sections.whyItMatters: This bill is unlikely to pass in its current form, but it signals that congressional patience with Ankara's human rights record remains thin. Combined with the existing F-35 congressional roadblock, it adds another friction point to a defense relationship that both sides need but neither can easily fix.

sections.heading: Erdogan Reaffirms Terror-Free Türkiye Initiative, Draft Legislation Nears Parliament
sections.body:
Speaking at an AK Party consultative council meeting in Istanbul on Saturday, President Erdogan said the Terror-Free Türkiye initiative had progressed 'without any setbacks' and pledged not to allow attempts to derail the process. He said terrorism had cost the country more than $2.3 trillion and tens of thousands of lives over nearly four decades. (SANA, Anadolu Agency)

Erdogan said draft legislative amendments tied to the initiative have been completed and will be submitted to parliament, potentially this week. As reported previously, Parliament Speaker Kurtulmus set an Aug. 14 deadline for a vote on the Terror-Free Türkiye bill before the summer recess. The bill would define the PKK as a defunct organization, place non-violent former members on five-year probation, and bar them from political office and public-sector employment. (Hurriyet Daily News)

Erdogan also highlighted the Development Road Project — a 1,200 km land corridor and railway connecting Iraq's Grand Faw Port to Turkiye and onward to Europe — as a top priority, framing it as central to regional economic integration. (SANA)
sections.whyItMatters: The legislative timeline is tightening. If the bill passes by Aug. 14, it creates a legal framework for PKK dissolution and reintegration — a turning point in Turkiye's 40-year conflict. The Development Road Project, meanwhile, connects the PKK process to economic logic: a stable southeast enables the transit corridor that makes Turkiye the overland bridge between the Gulf and Europe.

sections.heading: Iran-Oman Hormuz Deal Near Finalization, But Sticking Points Remain
sections.body:
Iranian Foreign Minister Araghchi confirmed that Oman-mediated negotiations over a 'mutual mechanism' for the Strait of Hormuz were in their final stages. Iranian officials said they showed openness to a Qatari proposal to create new traffic patterns for ships transiting the strait. However, Iran has insisted on controlling at least part of both shipping lanes and collecting tolls — a condition the US has rejected. (News18, Arab Times, FT via OilPrice.com)

Iran's Acting Defense Minister Seyed Majid Ebn Al-Reza said Sunday that Tehran perceives every 'enemy' threat seriously and would not remain passive if attacked. Araghchi separately held calls with counterparts in Saudi Arabia, Turkiye, and Pakistan to discuss the diplomatic push. (The Hans India, MSN)

For Turkiye, a Hormuz reopening — even with Iranian-controlled tolls — would ease the energy supply shock. But any deal that gives Tehran a permanent revenue stream from the strait would create a precedent Ankara would watch carefully, given its own maritime interests in the eastern Mediterranean. (USA Today, News18)
sections.whyItMatters: The Oman-Iran Hormuz talks are the most consequential development for Turkiye's energy security right now. If they succeed, oil prices drop further and the lira gets breathing room. If they fail, Turkiye's Ceyhan bypass becomes even more valuable — and more contested.

sections.heading: Gulf States Push Back on Escalation as Houthi Strikes Continue
sections.body:
Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Qatar all urged Trump to hold off on strikes, according to Trump himself. The Saudi Foreign Ministry said the crown prince's call with Trump sought clarity on Washington's broader strategy and urged dialogue to prevent escalation into a wider regional conflict. Gulf states have grown frustrated with the absence of a clear US strategy, WSJ reported, and have requested more air-defense interceptors and continued protection guarantees. (News18, WSJ via Fox News)

Houthi attacks on Saudi oil facilities and the Saudi shipping blockade in the Red Sea continue. Three additional tanker attacks were reported over the weekend. Nigeria and Bangladesh have joined the Saudi-led Red Sea defence coalition, expanding the multinational maritime security arrangement. (Reuters, The Nation, MSN)

Turkiye joined the Saudi-led Red Sea coalition on Aug. 1, as reported in our previous brief. The coalition now includes over a dozen nations, but its practical effectiveness against Houthi strikes remains unproven. (Hurriyet Daily News)
sections.whyItMatters: Gulf states' intervention to stop the strikes reveals a shift in influence: they now hold more sway over Trump than Israel does, according to Israeli intelligence analysts cited by WSJ. For Turkiye, being part of the Red Sea coalition and positioned as a diplomatic mediator gives Ankara relevance — but it also means exposure to retaliation if the conflict escalates further.

bottomLine: Monday is a pivotal day: US-Iran talks resume after Trump called off massive strikes, oil has dropped 5% on de-escalation hopes, and Oman-mediated Hormuz negotiations are reportedly in their final stages. For Turkiye, every one of these developments is existential — the lira's trajectory, energy costs, and the strategic value of the Ceyhan corridor all hinge on whether diplomacy holds. Domestically, the Terror-Free Türkiye bill is heading to parliament with an Aug. 14 deadline, and a new US Congress bill targeting Ankara's arms sales adds another layer of friction to the defense relationship. The gap between Trump's optimism and Tehran's public posture means Monday's talks could go either way.
sources: Fox News, USA Today, Reuters, OilPrice.com, MSN, News18, Arab Times, Zee News, SANA, Anadolu Agency, Hurriyet Daily News, Greek Reporter, Digital Journal, Bloomberg, The Hans India, WSJ, The Nation, AFR, CNN
